claim: An EMG-informed extended-DMP framework can jointly learn and goal-generalize demonstrated motion and impedance profiles; bounded Baxter experiments indicate that raising terminal stiffness improved cutting and that a generalized stiffness schedule improved heavy-object lift-place success.
epistemic_status: bounded primary experimental evidence; platform- and task-specific, without inferential statistics or formal guarantees
problem_and_setting: Robot learning from demonstration often transfers position trajectories without human stiffness, limiting generalization in physical-interaction tasks. Tests used a dual-arm Baxter with one calibrated tutor in cutting and obstacle-constrained lift-place tasks.
method_or_mechanism: MYO upper-limb EMG estimates a tutor endpoint-stiffness indicator, which is mapped to robot impedance gains. An extended DMP encodes trajectory and stiffness profiles; changing goal parameters generalizes spatial endpoints and/or terminal stiffness. Multiple demonstrations are combined using qualitatively selected weights, and the slave arm executes through PD impedance.
content_summary: Ten cutting demonstrations supported spatial cut-location generalization. Hard-object cutting success across five trials was 0/5 at terminal stiffness 0.65, 1/5 at 0.8, and 5/5 at 0.9. In seven-trial lift-place subtasks, the demonstrated object/stiffness condition achieved 7/7, the heavier object without a stiffness schedule 1/7, and the heavier object with generalized stiffness 6/7.
synthesis_role: Primary evidence that variable-impedance skill representations can couple motion and stiffness learning and use stiffness-goal adaptation to improve task success under changed interaction demands.
development_link: Supports development of impedance-aware learning-from-demonstration methods while motivating probabilistic demonstration fusion, multi-tutor validation, comparative baselines, and stability/safety analysis.

evidence.finding: Generalized cucumber cut locations were reproduced from ten demonstrations.
Success increased from 0/5 at terminal stiffness 0.65 to 1/5 at 0.8 and 5/5 at 0.9; force/position plots were reported as showing that higher stiffness enabled cutting.
Success was 7/7 for the demonstrated object/stiffness, 1/7 for a 1.40 kg object without the stiffness schedule, and 6/7 with generalized stiffness.

boundary_conditions: Five cutting trials per stiffness goal
No formal stability analysis or force/safety certificate
assumptions: EMG measurements provide a sufficiently accurate stiffness estimate.
The stiffness indicator-to-impedance-gain mapping is appropriate for the tested robot and tasks.
Observed condition differences are attributable mainly to the generalized stiffness schedule despite limited controls.

reported: Hard-object cutting failed 5/5 times at reference stiffness 0.65 and 4/5 times at 0.8.
Heavy-object lift-place without a stiffness schedule failed 6/7 times.
EMG-derived reference quality depends on signal and stiffness-estimation accuracy.
inferred: The small, non-randomized task-specific trials do not establish general effectiveness or statistical reliability.
The claimed easy transfer to other platforms and applications is untested.
Safety, robustness to unseen tutors, and closed-loop stability remain unresolved.

verification_status: Controller-verified replay identity, full-text access, and PDF SHA-256; findings extracted only from the supplied packet.
